title: Generated: One whole, equal units

prompts: After seven days, independently explain: Represent fractions, including fractions equal to or greater than 1, on area models and a number line, naming the whole each fraction refers to.
Apply the idea to a new context and justify the evidence or calculations used. This is a request for a governed retention task, not a scheduled or scored item.

pedagogy.rationale: Generate representations and worked reasoning from a versioned subject plan, then fade support before independent work and transfer.

prerequisiteAssumptions: Can read or access the text equivalent and explain a response in writing or speech.

misconceptions.description: Adds denominators or treats a rounded decimal as an exact fraction.
misconceptions.response: Preserve the whole and rename in equal-sized pieces. Distinguish exact equality from an explicitly requested approximation.

scenes.title: One whole, equal units
scenes.learnerAction: Sketch 1 and 3/2 on equal bars and on a number line. Name the whole and explain why 3/2 exceeds 1.

content.body: Use one bar as one kilogram. Equal parts must have the same size. Five fourths fills one whole bar and one quarter of another equal bar. On a number line, each interval of length one is one whole. Locate 5/4 between 1 and 2.

scenes.title: Rename before combining
scenes.learnerAction: Use the model, complete its task, and explain what the representation shows.

content.body: An exact fraction is the primary answer. Equivalent fractions such as 5/6 and 10/12 are equally correct. A finite decimal is equivalent only when exactly equal, such as 3/4 = 0.75. Here 5/6 is not equal to 0.83. Only a question explicitly requesting rounding accepts 0.83 as an approximation to two decimal places.

accessibility.textAlternative: An exact fraction is the primary answer. Equivalent fractions such as 5/6 and 10/12 are equally correct. A finite decimal is equivalent only when exactly equal, such as 3/4 = 0.75. Here 5/6 is not equal to 0.83. Only a question explicitly requesting rounding accepts 0.83 as an approximation to two decimal places. Add 1/2 and 1/3 of the same kilogram. Step 1: Rename both amounts in sixths. 1/2 = 3/6, 1/3 = 2/6 Step 2: Count pieces of the same size; keep the denominator. 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6 Order 1/2, 2/3 and 3/4. Step 1: On the same whole, use twelfths and the benchmarks zero, one half and one. 1/2 = 6/12, 2/3 = 8/12, 3/4 = 9/12 Step 2: Count equal intervals from zero. 1/2 < 2/3 < 3/4 < 1

content.body: Draw equal wholes, rename related denominators and write an exact fraction before choosing. To add like denominators, add only the counts. To subtract, remove that many equal pieces. A denominator describes the piece size, not a second count to add.

scenes.title: Measure seed exactly
scenes.learnerAction: Give the exact remaining mass and the approximation to two decimal places. Explain why the remainder is positive and smaller than 3/4 kg.

content.body: Synthetic seed-bank task. A group has 3/4 kg and packs 1/3 kg. Write the exact remainder as a fraction and justify its size. Then, as a separate estimate, round the remainder to two decimal places, using the third decimal digit and rounding a halfway value up. Write approximately equal for the estimate.
